summary: For ages 5-6, this is the seed of noticing that a calculation or move REPEATS and using that to count more efficiently or predict, rather than starting afresh each time. Children learn that adding 1 always gives the next counting number, that skip-counting in 2s from 2 lands on every second number (the even numbers, skipping the odd ones between), and that on a standard hundred square with 1 in the top row, +10 moves you straight down one row whenever there is a row below. The teaching job is to prompt the child to expect the repeat and test it ('will it happen again?'), not to hand over the rule. The most developed activity has the child predict the next repeat and then see it happen; recognition checks and highlighted references play supporting roles.
misconceptions: Counts in ones every time instead of using the repeated +10 move, treating each sum as brand new
Sees a pattern work once but does not expect it to continue, so won't use it to predict
Loses the skip-count structure partway (2, 4, 6, 8, 9) by reverting to counting in ones
Thinks 'the next number' and 'one more' are unrelated ideas rather than the same repeated +1

activities.title: Predict-the-jump hundred square
steps: Point to 24 on a hundred square.
Before moving anything, say out loud where you think 24 + 10 will land.
Move a counter straight down one row to land on 34 and check your guess.
Do it again: predict 34 + 10, then land on 44; then predict 44 + 10 and land on 54.
After a few jumps, try to say where the next +10 will land without looking closely — notice you no longer need to recount.
Try a jump from a different starting number (e.g. 'will adding ten from 57 still go straight down a row? shall we check?') to test whether the repeat always holds.
activities.insight: On this hundred square (1 in the top row), adding ten moves you straight down one row each time there is a row below, so once you notice the repeat you can predict the next result instead of counting ten squares each time.

activities.title: Skip-count rhythm track
steps: Count in 2s along a number track or line of steps: 2, 4, 6, 8, ...
Add a steady beat (clap, drum, or stepping) on each number so the repeating rhythm is heard as well as seen.
After a few steps, try to call the next number before you reach it.
Notice which numbers you land on and which you skip; talk about the odd/even alternation.
Answer: 'Is 7 in your counting-by-2s? Why not?' and 'What comes after 2, 4, 6, 8 — how did you know without counting all of them?'
activities.insight: Skip-counting in 2s follows a repeating, predictable rhythm with a steady even pattern, so you can anticipate the next number instead of counting in ones.

activities.title: Distinguish the +1 move from the +10 move
steps: On the hundred square, show where adding 1 takes you from a number — usually one place to the right, to the next counting number (at the end of a row it continues at the start of the next row).
Then show where adding 10 takes you (straight down one row).
Optionally, use a ten-frame: add one counter and see the total become the next number — the same steady 'one more' step.
Say in your own words how the two moves are different.
Connect 'the next number' and 'one more': confirm these are the same repeated +1 move.
activities.insight: Different repeated moves have different fixed effects: +1 gives the next counting number, +10 drops down a row. 'One more' and 'the next number' are the same idea, not unrelated.

activities.title: Light check: what comes next in the sequence
steps: Say how you knew without counting from the start.
activities.insight: Being able to continue the sequence and explain the repeat shows the pattern was genuinely noticed.

checkQuestion: Here is 24 on the hundred square. Without counting, where will 34 be? And 44? How do you know where to look each time?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child using the repeated move: 'adding ten goes straight down a row every time, so 34 is under 24 and 44 is under that.' The expectation that the move REPEATS is the target, not the cell.
